title: How to work cross-stitch on evenweave
subtitle: Stitching over two threads on 28-count Jobelan and similar fabrics
excerpt: Evenweave fabrics for cross-stitch are synthetic or cotton-and-linen weaves with a uniform thread count in both directions, worked over two threads like linen but with more consistency and slightly stiffer handling than natural linen. The most common evenweave used for cross-stitch is 28-count Jobelan.
sourceNotes: Evenweave cross-stitch conventions follow the same over-two method as natural linen. Widely documented in modern needlework guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fabric woven with the same number of threads per centimetre in both warp and weft directions. Used for cross-stitch worked over two threads, giving consistent stitch proportions. Common counts are 22, 25, and 28.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
A blunt-tipped needle that slips between fabric threads instead of piercing them. Size 24 is the default for 14ct Aida; finer fabrics need a higher-number, finer needle.

content.text: fabrics are woven with the same thread count across and down, so each stitch worked over two threads is a true square. This is the fabric to choose between
and linen: it has the regularity that makes counting straightforward, but it drapes better than Aida and gives a softer finished piece.
Working on evenweave is the same as working on linen. Each cross covers two threads in each direction, and the needle passes between threads rather than through Aida holes. A size 24 or 26
suits most evenweave counts. The main difference from linen is that synthetic and cotton-blend evenweaves are stiffer, with larger gaps between threads. This makes the over-two path easier to follow.
Standard needle and thread choices for common evenweave counts:
22-count evenweave (over two = 11-count equivalent): size 22 needle, three strands of floss
25-count evenweave (over two = 12.5-count equivalent): size 24 needle, two strands of floss
28-count evenweave (over two = 14-count equivalent): size 24 needle, two strands of floss
Identify the first stitch on the chart. Find the corresponding position on the fabric by counting from the basted centre line.
Come up between thread 1 and thread 2 (counting from the left edge of the planned first stitch) in both the horizontal and vertical directions. This is the bottom-left corner of the first cross.
Take the lower diagonal over two threads in each direction. Enter between threads 3 and 4 in the horizontal direction and threads 3 and 4 in the vertical direction (the top-right corner).
Complete the return diagonal to form the full cross. Each stitch should look as even as on Aida; if stitches are irregular, re-count whether two threads are being covered each time.

items.symptom: Stitches look elongated, taller than they are wide
items.cause: The fabric is not a true evenweave, or the thread count is different in the two directions.
items.fix: Check the fabric specification. True evenweave has the same count in both directions. If the stitch count differs, stitches worked over two threads will not be square.

content.text: Once comfortable on 28-count evenweave, linen is the natural progression. The technique is identical, but the texture and drape of natural linen make a noticeably softer finished piece for framing.
